column1: # Templates for OpenCode's permission.bash keys (FEAT-042 T4), expanded by
# opencode-guard.sh. One row per line, tab separated, no empty field:
#   id    a rule id of guardrail-rules.sh (see tests/guard-corpus.tsv)
#   kind  deny | ask        <rest> is a template: it expands to permission.bash keys
#         untranslatable    <rest> is the reason (what no key can express), which
#         miss              <rest> is a corpus command (a JSON string) of that rule that
#                           the keys do NOT stop, TAB, why
#         over              the same, for a command the shell guard lets through and the
# A template is the glob, with these placeholders expanded to every value:
#                 {DISK}  sd nvme disk vd hd mmcblk
# How OpenCode 1.18.31 reads a key (MEASURED with `opencode debug agent build --tool
# bash`, payload/test/cli-guard.sh CF-46; the docs say less):
#   - `*` is any run of characters (spaces included), the key is anchored at both ends, and
#     a trailing " *" is optional (`mkfs *` also matches a bare `mkfs`);
#   - the command is cut into its simple commands first (at ; && || | & and newlines, and
#     inside $( ), ( ) and backticks) and EVERY piece is matched on its own, so a key can
#     never see a pipe: `curl x | sudo bash` is two commands to the engine;
#   - a piece starts at its first word: `sudo rm -rf /` is not matched by `rm -rf /`
#     (hence {PRE}), and quotes are part of the text: `rm -rf "/"` is not matched by
#   - a redirect is part of its command's text (`cat x > /dev/sda` is one piece);
#   - the LAST matching key wins: all `ask` keys come first, then all `deny` keys.
# `ask` cannot be observed through `debug agent` (it answers yes to every ask), so only
# the deny keys are checked against the real engine.
# The flag globs are wide on purpose: -*r*f* is -rf -fr -vrf -rfv "-r -f" and
# --recursive --force; -*f*r* is the same the other way round. Anything that ends with the
# target as a word is a deletion of the target, so the over-blocking is harmless.
